record.narrative: This is an initial broad, biologically motivated wave focusing on high-prior binary predictors that are likely to show meaningful associations with CRISPR dependency scores. More negative dependency means stronger dependence, so claims with direction -1 expect a more negative score in the exposed group, whereas direction +1 expects a less negative/positive score. I prioritize canonical oncogene-dependency relationships: KRAS mutation with KRAS dependency, BRAF V600E with BRAF dependency, EGFR amplification with EGFR dependency, and ERBB2 amplification with ERBB2 dependency. I also test whether KRAS mutation extends to nearby RAS-pathway dependency on RIT1. Synthetic-lethality and pathway-specific hypotheses are included: MDM2 and USP7 dependencies should be weaker in TP53-loss lines because p53-proficient cells are typically more sensitive to p53 regulators; WRN dependency should be stronger in MSI-high lines; NFE2L2 dependency should be stronger in KEAP1-loss lines because KEAP1 loss activates the NRF2/NFE2L2 axis; SMARCA2 dependency should be stronger in SMARCA4-deficient lines due to SWI/SNF paralog dependence. Finally, MYC amplification is tested as a marker of transcriptional addiction, with predicted stronger DHX9 and POLR2A dependencies. These analyses will identify which predictor-outcome pairs are worth focused follow-up; later waves can assess research signatures, marker assays, culture/library effects, and interaction/subgroup refinements.

Running the full first wave of 12 registered high-prior comparisons, covering canonical oncogene dependencies, p53-pathway dependencies, MSI/WRN, KEAP1/NFE2L2, SWI/SNF/SMARCA2, and MYC/transcriptional dependencies. These provide discovery evidence on effect size and uncertainty for the most biologically plausible predictor-outcome pairs.

Sign convention matters here: for direction -1, a positive signed estimate corresponds to a raw exposed-minus-comparator difference that is negative, i.e. stronger dependency in the exposed group; for direction +1, a positive signed estimate corresponds to a raw positive difference, i.e. weaker/less negative dependency. The three strongest results are H7, H8, and H10. H7 shows TP53-loss lines have much weaker USP7 dependency than TP53-intact lines: signed estimate +0.802 (95% interval +0.782 to +0.822), a huge effect relative to the outcome scale and far above the 10% clinical-significance threshold. H8 shows MSI-high lines have much stronger WRN dependency than non-MSI-high lines: signed estimate +0.790 (interval +0.760 to +0.819), also very large. H10 shows SMARCA4-loss lines have much stronger SMARCA2 dependency: signed estimate +0.784 (interval +0.765 to +0.803). I accept these as scientifically meaningful associations within this dataset, while noting they are observational cell-line associations and could be confounded by co-mutations, lineage subtype, culture/library effects, or batch; validation and subgroup/stratification analyses are needed before stronger causal or generalizable claims. H3 is the most interesting borderline result: EGFR-amplified lines have a nominally stronger EGFR dependency, signed estimate +0.0252, but the interval crosses zero very slightly (signed interval -0.00025 to +0.0507) and the point estimate is only around 10% relative to the typical EGFR dependency scale. This is unresolved and I request independent validation before accepting. H9 contradicts the original hypothesis strongly: KEAP1-loss lines have weaker, not stronger, NFE2L2 dependency; the signed estimate is -0.796 (interval -0.816 to -0.776), which corresponds to a raw positive difference of about +0.80 against the expected negative direction. I reject H9 but register a reversed claim as a new hypothesis. H1, H2, H4, H5, H6, H11, and H12 show point estimates well below the clinically meaningful 10% scale and intervals including zero, with no directional support strong enough to justify acceptance; I reject and close them unless robustness analyses suggest otherwise. The next wave prioritizes the reversed NFE2L2/KEAP1 relationship, robustness of the three large effects within adenocarcinoma, and negative-control/technical-marker checks to assess whether large associations might be driven by nonbiological marker or assay effects.

The independent validation for H3 does not support EGFR amplification as a meaningful predictor of EGFR dependency in this dataset. The discovery signed estimate was +0.0252 (95% interval -0.00025 to +0.0507), barely favoring stronger dependency but not excluding no effect. The validation signed estimate was -0.0221 (independent interval -0.0614 to +0.0172), i.e. the opposite direction, while still including no effect. The two estimates are not consistent, and the magnitude is small relative to the 10% clinical-significance benchmark; therefore H3 is rejected as a supported association. The large discovery effects for H7, H8, H10, and the reversed NFE2L2/KEAP1 relationship H13 remain accepted as dataset-level associations. H13 is now accepted because, when the direction was reversed from the original biological hypothesis, the same direct evidence shows a very large and precise effect: KEAP1-loss lines have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency than KEAP1-intact lines (signed estimate +0.796, 95% interval +0.776 to +0.816). This is a post hoc direction correction based on the observed data, but the effect is far beyond the 10% benchmark and far from null; it is still only an observational association in this cell-line dataset, not causal proof. For the accepted large effects, the main uncertainties are confounding and generalizability: lineage subtype, co-occurring TP53/KEAP1/MSI/SMARCA4 states, culture or library artifacts, and research-marker assay effects could explain or modify them. The next wave therefore prioritizes (1) replication of the four large associations within adenocarcinoma, (2) interaction tests asking whether adenocarcinoma versus complement differ, (3) co-occurrence checks by restricting each exposure to lines without the other major predictor, and (4) research-marker/library controls to detect nonbiological driver patterns. If these robustness and negative-control analyses do not reveal technical artifacts, independent validation can be used sparingly on one of the accepted large effects, but the most immediate informative work is subgroup/co-mutation decomposition rather than more borderline single-marker tests.

The first wave supports four very large dataset-level associations: KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency. Before treating these as broadly meaningful or interpretable, I want to determine whether they are robust to the strongest plausible confounders and whether they are predictor-specific. The first four new proposals replicate each accepted effect in lines lacking the other major genetic states: NFE2L2 in TP53-intact/MSS lines, USP7 in KEAP1-intact/MSS lines, SMARCA2 in TP53-intact/KEAP1-intact/MSS lines, and WRN in TP53-intact/KEAP1-intact lines. If these co-occurrence-restricted estimates remain large and directional, they are less likely to be driven only by co-mutation mixture. The library-Avana controls and marker controls test whether the large dependencies are artifacts of screen batch/library or constructed marker assays; for these controls I use the signed direction matching the accepted association for that outcome, so a large positive signed effect would raise concern about a shared technical or latent cell-state driver. The interaction controls test whether the accepted genetic effects differ within marker-defined subgroups, again probing artifact or modification. The cross-pathway specificity tests ask whether KEAP1 loss also moves USP7 and whether SMARCA4 loss also moves WRN; strong cross-effects would suggest a non-specific latent factor rather than pathway-specific dependence. I am not requesting validation yet: validation is more useful after these robustness and artifact screens, and should be reserved for associations that remain large and stable.

Selecting twelve untested claims that most directly interrogate the four accepted large associations. First, the co-occurrence-restricted replicas H29-H32 test whether each accepted effect remains large when the other major genetic states are excluded: KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 dependency among TP53-intact/MSS lines, TP53-loss USP7 dependency among KEAP1-intact/MSS lines, SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 dependency among TP53-intact/KEAP1-intact/MSS lines, and MSI-high WRN dependency among TP53-intact/KEAP1-intact lines. These are key confounding checks for the possibility that one accepted effect is merely a proxy for another co-mutation state. Second, the library-Avana controls H20 and H33-H35 test whether large differences for WRN, NFE2L2, SMARCA2, and USP7 can be produced by the dominant CRISPR library/technical batch variable; large technical contrasts in the same signed direction would caution that the accepted associations may be screen-technology artifacts or latent batch-correlated cell-state effects. Third, marker controls H18 and H36 test whether constructed marker assays F and E track SMARCA2 or NFE2L2 dependencies directly; strong marker effects would suggest a non-biological constructed-marker artifact and would lower confidence in the corresponding accepted association. Fourth, cross-pathway specificity checks H41 and H42 test whether KEAP1 loss moves USP7 and whether SMARCA4 loss moves WRN. If these cross-associations are small or inconsistent, the accepted associations look more pathway-specific; if they are also very large, a shared latent factor or artifact becomes more plausible. I am not running marker interaction or lineage interaction tests yet; those are deferred until main marker/library and co-occurrence results clarify which accepted effects remain credible.

The co-occurrence-restricted replication is very informative. H29 keeps the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 result within lines that are TP53-intact and MSS: KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, signed estimate +0.795, 95% interval +0.771 to +0.818. H30 similarly preserves the TP53/USP7 association among KEAP1-intact, MSS lines, signed estimate +0.802, interval +0.779 to +0.826. H31 preserves the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 association among TP53-intact, KEAP1-intact, MSS lines, signed estimate +0.784, interval +0.759 to +0.808. H32 preserves the MSI-high/WRN association among TP53-intact and KEAP1-intact lines, signed estimate +0.774, interval +0.736 to +0.813, despite a smaller exposed cell_n of 81. These restricted estimates are all far larger than the 10% clinical-significance benchmark and show that the accepted large associations are not simple proxies for one another or limited to lines containing the other major genetic state. They still remain observational cell-line associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

The artifact and specificity screens are reassuring. The dominant CRISPR library indicator is not associated with large outcome shifts in the same signed direction as the accepted claims: H20 WRN versus Avana estimate -0.022, H33 NFE2L2 estimate +0.036, H34 SMARCA2 estimate +0.051, and H35 USP7 estimate +0.046; all intervals include zero and point estimates are small relative to the accepted effects of roughly 0.78-0.80. The upper bound for H34 slightly exceeds 0.10, but the non-significant point is modest and does not resemble the magnitude of the accepted SMARCA4/SMARCA2 effect. Constructed markers are not strong direct drivers: H18 SMARCA2 versus marker F estimate -0.015 and H36 NFE2L2 versus marker E estimate +0.001, both with intervals near zero. Cross-pathway specificity is also consistent with pathway-specific associations: H41 KEAP1 loss versus USP7 estimate +0.009 and H42 SMARCA4 loss versus WRN estimate +0.003 are small and non-directional. I reject these negative-control and cross-effect claims as scientifically meaningful associations and close them. These controls do not prove absence of technical confounding; they mainly show that no direct marker or library effect of comparable magnitude was detected. Residual confounding through correlated library/genotype distributions, batch, culture conditions, or other latent states remains possible.

Given that the large associations have now passed direct artifact screens and co-occurrence robustness checks, I request independent validation for H13, the KEAP1-loss/weaker-NFE2L2-dependency association. This is the most consequential unresolved issue because it required a reversal of the original biological hypothesis and because post hoc direction reversal deserves independent confirmation. If validation reproduces a positive signed effect, H13 becomes a more credible dataset-level association. If validation does not reproduce it, H13 should be downgraded and the subgroup/interaction analyses will become the priority. I selected H13 rather than H7, H8, or H10 for this validation slot because H13 is the most surprising and most likely to be affected by dataset-specific structure.

The independent validation for H13 strongly supports the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 association. H13 was registered after the original H9 hypothesis was contradicted by discovery data, so this is a post hoc directional claim; however, the validation now confirms it. The validation signed estimate is +0.806 with an independent interval of +0.775 to +0.838, excluding zero under a stringent validation threshold and far exceeding the 10% clinical-significance benchmark. Because dependency scores are more negative when dependency is stronger, a positive signed estimate under direction +1 means KEAP1-loss lines have much less negative NFE2L2 scores, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. This is consistent with the discovery estimate of +0.796 and with the co-occurrence-restricted estimate of +0.795 in TP53-intact/MSS lines. I therefore accept H13 as a scientifically meaningful dataset-level association, while H9 remains rejected because the same evidence confirms the opposite of its original expected stronger NFE2L2 dependency. The current evidence base now separates three layers: validated broad association, accepted but not independently validated associations, and negative/artifact controls. The accepted broad effects are H13 KEAP1 loss associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, H7 TP53 loss associated with weaker USP7 dependency, H8 MSI-high associated with stronger WRN dependency, and H10 SMARCA4 loss associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Their restricted robustness claims H29-H32 also remain accepted, with estimated effects of roughly +0.77 to +0.80 even after excluding lines with the other major genetic states. The artifact screens did not support a large marker-F, marker-E, library-Avana, or cross-pathway effect: H18, H36, H20, H33-H35, H41, and H42 are rejected as meaningful associations. H3 is also a clear negative finding: EGFR amplification had a borderline positive discovery effect but opposite validation effect, so the evidence does not support EGFR amplification as a meaningful predictor of EGFR dependency in this dataset. Remaining uncertainty is mainly generalizability and residual confounding rather than effect size for the accepted effects: H7, H8, and H10 still lack independent validation, and all four accepted effects could still be modified by lineage subtype, screen batch, culture condition, age, sex, or other latent cell-state variables. The most informative next analysis is therefore the remaining robustness and interaction panel: lineage-specific replication in adenocarcinoma, Avana versus non-Avana robustness, batch-a interaction tests, marker interaction/main controls, and pathway-inspired specificity tests such as ARID1A loss with SMARCA2 dependency and TP53 loss with RPL11 dependency. If these subgroup tests remain broadly consistent, the next validation request should target one canonical accepted effect, likely H10 SMARCA4 loss associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency; if heterogeneity is large, interaction analysis should take priority over additional validation.

No assessments are due at this stage. The next wave is organized around three complementary goals. First, I registered conditional follow-ups for the accepted large associations in the presence of another major genetic state: KEAP1-loss effect on NFE2L2 within TP53-loss lines, TP53-loss effect on USP7 within KEAP1-loss lines, and SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 within TP53-loss lines. These ask whether the accepted effects persist in alternative co-mutation contexts rather than only in lines that lack the other major state. Second, I registered robustness and interaction tests using measurable technical and demographic subgroups that have not yet been interrogated: high screen ROC quality for KEAP1/NFE2L2, male sex for TP53/USP7, adherent culture for SMARCA4/SMARCA2, and high serum for MSI/WRN. These test whether the very large associations are generalized across screen quality, sex, culture configuration, and medium serum, or whether they are driven or modified by these subgroup factors. Third, I registered cross-pathway specificity controls: TP53-loss and KEAP1-loss with SMARCA2, and SMARCA4-loss with USP7. If these are also very large, the accepted effects would be less specific and more compatible with a shared latent cell-state or technical factor; if small, the pathway-specific pattern remains more credible. Finally, I added broader discovery hypotheses for previously untested outcomes and canonical pathway variables: PIK3CA mutation and PTEN loss with STAT3 dependency, MYC amplification with RPL11 dependency, RB1 and CDKN2A loss with KIF18A dependency, and ERBB2 amplification with TMED10 dependency. These are falsifiable and biologically motivated, but they remain exploratory unless the signed estimate is large, precise, and consistent with the hypothesized direction. All results will be interpreted as dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

Selecting twelve new analyses to interrogate robustness, heterogeneity, and pathway specificity of the four accepted large associations. First, H25-H28 request interaction tests by lineage subtype (adenocarcinoma vs complement) for SMARCA2/SMARCA4, WRN/MSI, USP7/TP53, and NFE2L2/KEAP1. These ask whether the accepted effects differ by subtype or are homogeneous across the measured subtype split. Because estimates are already signed to the hypothesis direction, a positive signed interaction would indicate the effect is stronger in adenocarcinoma than in the complement, whereas a negative signed interaction would indicate it is weaker. Second, H52-H55 request analogous screen_batch_a interactions for the same four accepted associations, testing whether a dominant technical/batch variable modifies the effects. Third, H56-H58 are co-mutation-restricted main effects: KEAP1-loss effect on NFE2L2 among TP53-loss lines, TP53-loss effect on USP7 among KEAP1-loss lines, and SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 among TP53-loss lines. These complement the earlier TP53/KEAP1/MSS-restricted tests and ask whether the effects persist when the exposure is considered within the presence of another major genetic state rather than only in lines lacking it. Fourth, H47 tests ARID1A loss versus SMARCA2 dependency as a BAF-complex specificity check: if ARID1A loss produces a comparable SMARCA2 shift, the association may reflect general SWI/SNF/BAF loss biology; if it does not, the SMARCA4-specific association remains more specific. I defer sex, culture, serum, marker, and other broad pathway tests until these heterogeneity and specificity screens clarify whether the accepted effects are stable enough to merit further validation.

The new interaction and conditional-effect panel largely supports the stability of the four accepted large associations while identifying one small, statistically detectable but clinically trivial batch interaction. For lineage subtype, all interaction estimates are close to zero and below the practical clinical-significance scale: H25 SMARCA4/SMARCA2 estimate -0.028 [-0.076, 0.020]; H26 MSI/WRN -0.021 [-0.085, 0.042]; H27 TP53/USP7 -0.010 [-0.053, 0.033]; H28 KEAP1/NFE2L2 -0.012 [-0.057, 0.033]. I therefore reject these lineage-subtype interaction claims as meaningful subgroup modifications. This does not prove complete homogeneity, but it gives no support for the accepted effects being driven only by adenocarcinoma versus the complement.  The screen-batch_a interactions are also small. H52 KEAP1/NFE2L2 +0.021 [-0.031, 0.072], H53 TP53/USP7 -0.019 [-0.064, 0.027], and H55 MSI/WRN +0.048 [-0.020, 0.115] have point estimates far below the 10%-or-0.1-scale benchmark and confidence intervals centered near zero. H54 SMARCA4/SMARCA2 is different in that its interval excludes zero, signed estimate -0.051 [-0.095, -0.007], but the magnitude is still small: it corresponds to a modest, opposite-signed batch modification and is only about 6% of the main SMARCA4/SMARCA2 effect. With many subgroup tests, I interpret this as statistically detectable but not clinically meaningful heterogeneity, and I reject it as a meaningful interaction.  The co-mutation-restricted main effects are very informative. H56, the KEAP1-loss effect on NFE2L2 dependency among TP53-loss lines, is strongly positive, signed estimate +0.810 [0.763, 0.857]; because the signed direction is +1, this indicates much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss lines even when TP53 is lost. H57, the TP53-loss effect on USP7 dependency among KEAP1-loss lines, is also large, +0.794 [0.754, 0.834], supporting weaker USP7 dependency in TP53-loss lines within KEAP1-loss contexts. H58, the SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 dependency among TP53-loss lines, is strong, +0.773 [0.729, 0.817], consistent with stronger SMARCA2 dependency in SMARCA4-loss lines. These conditional effects are all far larger than the clinical benchmark and indicate that the accepted effects are not limited to lines lacking another major genetic state. They remain observational dataset-level associations, not causal effects.  The pathway-specificity check H47 rejects ARID1A loss as an alternative broad BAF-complex explanation for the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 association: signed estimate -0.017 [-0.057, 0.023]. Since ARID1A loss is not associated with SMARCA2 dependency of comparable magnitude, the accepted SMARCA4/SMARCA2 effect remains more specific to SMARCA4 loss than to generalized BAF loss.  Overall, this panel strengthens confidence in the accepted effects: no lineage interaction is clinically meaningful; batch effects are mostly negligible, with one small SMARCA4/SMARCA2 modification; co-mutation-restricted effects remain very large; and an ARID1A control does not reproduce the SMARCA2 effect. I therefore request independent validation for H10, the SMARCA4-loss association with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, because it is canonical, pathway-specific, and now supported by direct co-occurrence and specificity checks. This validation will not establish causality or generalizability, but it would materially strengthen the dataset-level evidence.

The independent validation of H10 is decisive. The signed validation estimate is +0.7925 with an independent interval of +0.763 to +0.822. Because H10 was registered with direction -1, a positive signed estimate corresponds to a negative exposed-minus-comparator difference in raw dependency units, i.e. SMARCA4-loss lines have substantially more negative SMARCA2 scores than SMARCA4-intact lines. Since more negative scores mean stronger CRISPR dependency, this confirms that SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in this dataset. The effect is far larger than the practical 10%-scale benchmark and is consistent with the discovery estimate (+0.784) and with restricted co-occurrence analyses (e.g., +0.784 in TP53/KEAP1/MSS lines and +0.773 among TP53-loss lines). I therefore accept H10 as a scientifically meaningful dataset-level association and close it as a canonical validated result. This does not establish causality or external generalizability, but it strengthens the dataset-level association. H10 is now independently validated alongside H13.

The H3 response deadline is also clear. Discovery gave a small signed estimate favoring EGFR amplification -> stronger EGFR dependency, but the validation estimate was opposite-signed and small (-0.022, interval -0.061 to +0.017). Across both discovery and validation the magnitude is well below the practical clinical-significance threshold and the evidence is inconsistent. Therefore EGFR amplification is not supported as a meaningful predictor of EGFR dependency in this dataset, and H3 remains rejected.

The next most informative work is not additional validation of the already validated canonical associations, but robustness across technical strata and screen quality, plus one leakage check for pathway specificity. I am keeping active the Avana-library effects for USP7/TP53, SMARCA2/SMARCA4, WRN/MSI, and NFE2L2/KEAP1; the non-Avana main effects for NFE2L2, USP7, and SMARCA2; a new non-Avana NFE2L2 effect; high screen-quality main effects for NFE2L2, USP7, SMARCA2, and WRN; and H63, which tests whether TP53 loss also shifts SMARCA2 dependency. I deferred lower-priority marker interactions, adenocarcinoma-only main effects because the corresponding lineage interactions were already small, sex/culture/serum interactions, other cross-specificity tests, and broad pathway discovery tests. This focused panel asks whether the large effects survive the dominant library split and high-quality screens, and whether they leak across pathways. After these results, the likely next validation target should be H8, MSI-high -> stronger WRN dependency, because its exposed cell size is smaller and independent validation would be most informative for a rare-subgroup synthetic-lethality-like association; H7 remains a secondary validation candidate.

No new discovery or validation evidence is due at this explore stage. The current evidence base strongly supports four dataset-level associations: KEAP1 loss associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency (validated), SMARCA4 loss associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency (validated), TP53 loss associated with weaker USP7 dependency, and MSI-high associated with stronger WRN dependency. The main remaining scientific questions are not whether these associations have large effects, but whether they are modified by major genetic co-states, screen-quality, or CRISPR library context, and whether they leak into biologically related dependencies. I therefore registered direct interaction tests rather than adding more subset main effects. First, I registered genetic-context interactions for the accepted effects: KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 modification by TP53-loss, TP53-loss/USP7 modification by KEAP1-loss, SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 modification by TP53-loss, and MSI-high/WRN modification by TP53-loss. These are more direct than comparing separate conditional main effects and test whether the associations behave homogeneously across TP53 or KEAP1 co-mutation status. Second, I registered screen-quality interactions using screen_roc_auc >= 0.93 versus the complement for all four accepted associations. This tests whether high-quality screens show the same effect magnitude as lower-quality screens, which is relevant to technical reliability. Third, I registered Avana-library interactions for KEAP1/NFE2L2, TP53/USP7, and SMARCA4/SMARCA2. I did not register a WRN library interaction because MSI-high within non-Avana lines is expected to be too small for stable Welch cells; for WRN, the broad and screen-quality interactions are more informative than a fragile library-stratified test. I deferred the previously registered library and screen-quality main-effect strata because the new interaction tests are more direct and statistically efficient for assessing modification. I also deferred TP53-loss with RPL11 dependency to keep the immediate focus on robustness of the four accepted large associations and one leakage control (H63, TP53-loss with SMARCA2 dependency). The accepted but validated or support conditional effects H29-H32 and H56-H58 are marked closed because they have served their purpose as supporting dataset-level associations; new refinements remain active. The anticipated direction for all new interactions is uncertain rather than assuming homogeneity, because the available conditional effects are large but not formally compared across complements. After these interaction results, if no clinically meaningful heterogeneity is found, the next independent validation candidate should be H8 MSI-high associated with stronger WRN dependency, because it is accepted, biologically interesting, and still lacks independent validation. If meaningful heterogeneity is found, the next priority should shift to refining the affected subgroup rather than validating a broad average effect. All conclusions remain dataset-level associations, not causal or broadly generalizable claims.

This run requests the twelve active registered comparisons that directly assess heterogeneity and leakage of the four large accepted associations: genetic-context interactions for KEAP1/NFE2L2, TP53/USP7, SMARCA4/SMARCA2, and MSI/WRN (H76-H79); screen-quality interactions using screen_roc_auc >= 0.93 for the same four associations (H80-H83); Avana-versus-non-Avana library interactions for KEAP1/NFE2L2, TP53/USP7, and SMARCA4/SMARCA2 (H84-H86); and the TP53-loss/SMARCA2 specificity control H63. These are chosen because the immediate scientific questions are whether the accepted large effects are stable across major co-mutation states, screen ROC quality, and the dominant library context, and whether they leak into neighboring dependency outcomes. The WRN-library interaction remains unrequested because MSI-high cells in non-Avana may be too sparse for stable Welch cells. If these interactions are near zero relative to the very large main effects, the broad dataset-level associations become more credible; if any interaction is large, follow-up should shift to subgroup-specific estimates before treating the broad average effect as the primary conclusion. All conclusions remain dataset-level associations, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

These twelve new results are secondary heterogeneity and specificity tests for the four large accepted associations. Their signed effect sizes are small compared with the main effects: H76 KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 interaction by TP53 loss is +0.0176 [-0.0340, 0.0693]; H77 TP53-loss/USP7 interaction by KEAP1 loss is -0.0100 [-0.0562, 0.0361]; H78 SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 interaction by TP53 loss is -0.0145 [-0.0636, 0.0345]; and H79 MSI-high/WRN interaction by TP53 loss is +0.0528 [-0.0215, 0.1272], where the latter is imprecise because the MSI-high/TP53-loss cell has n=24. The screen-quality interactions are also small: H80 +0.0042 [-0.0412, 0.0497], H81 +0.0255 [-0.0212, 0.0723], H82 +0.0218 [-0.0250, 0.0685], and H83 +0.0126 [-0.0659, 0.0911]. The Avana-library interactions are similarly small: H84 +0.0022 [-0.0506, 0.0550], H85 +0.0383 [-0.0292, 0.1057], and H86 -0.0198 [-0.0762, 0.0365]. None provides statistically or clinically meaningful evidence of effect modification on the 0.1-scale dependency benchmark; where intervals are wider, the point estimates remain far below the main effects and the evidence is not significant. I therefore reject all interaction claims as meaningful subgroup modifications and close them. The leakage/specificity control H63 is essentially null: signed estimate -0.00057 [-0.0407, 0.0396]. TP53 loss is not associated with SMARCA2 dependency, so this rejects a broad shared cell-state or pathway leakage explanation and supports the specificity of the accepted TP53/USP7 and SMARCA4/SMARCA2 associations. Collectively, this panel strengthens confidence that the broad dataset-level effects for H7, H8, H10, and H13 are not driven by major genetic co-states, screen-quality, or the dominant CRISPR library split. These remain dataset-level associations, not causal or externally generalizable claims. Given the small exposed subgroup for MSI-high WRN and the robustness of its interactions, the most valuable next independent check is validation of H8.

H13 response deadline is resolved decisively by independent validation. The signed validation estimate for KEAP1 loss on NFE2L2 dependency is +0.8065 with an independent interval of +0.7754 to +0.8376. Because H13 is direction +1, this is a raw positive shift: KEAP1-loss lines have much more positive NFE2L2 scores, meaning substantially weaker dependency. The interval is tight, wholly away from zero and from any trivial range, and it matches discovery +0.7961 [0.7759, 0.8163]. I therefore keep H13 accepted and close it as a validated dataset-level association. H8 validation is equally decisive. The signed estimate for MSI-high on WRN dependency is +0.8019, independent interval +0.7533 to +0.8506. Because H8 is direction -1, a positive signed value corresponds to a raw negative shift: MSI-high lines have much more negative WRN scores, meaning much stronger WRN dependency. This is consistent with discovery +0.7899 [0.7604, 0.8193] and far exceeds the practical 10% clinical-significance benchmark. I therefore accept H8 as a scientifically meaningful, independently validated dataset-level association and close it. The earlier interaction panel showed no clinically meaningful modification by lineage, screen quality, library, or TP53/KEAP1 co-states for these large effects, and pathway-specificity controls did not suggest simple leakage. I am therefore moving from validating already-settled associations to broadening the search across remaining outcomes and plausible predictors. I activated H48 RPL11/TP53, H66 STAT3/PIK3CA, H67 STAT3/PTEN, H69 KIF18A/RB1, H70 KIF18A/CDKN2A, and H71 TMED10/ERBB2, and registered six new binary exposure tests covering STAT3/MYC, KIF18A/MYC, TMED10/EGFR, TMED10/PIK3CA, DHX9/TP53, and POLR2A/TP53. H7 TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency remains the only accepted large association lacking independent validation and is the next natural validation candidate at a later appraise stage. All conclusions remain dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

No new evidence is due, so the exploratory priority is to keep the immediate analysis budget focused on new, mechanistically plausible dependencies rather than further stratifying already-settled canonical effects. The validated dataset-level associations are KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency. H7 TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency remains the most important accepted association lacking independent validation, but validation is better considered after the new broad discovery panel returns because a newly discovered large association could become a more urgent validation target. To keep exactly twelve active comparisons for the next analyze stage, I defer two lower-priority TMED10 tests: TMED10 with EGFR amplification and TMED10 with PIK3CA mutation. EGFR amplification has already been weakly inconsistent for EGFR dependency, PIK3CA is still being tested for STAT3, and these TMED10 hypotheses are less mechanistically direct. I add two more focused comparisons. First, dependency_TMED10 by KRAS mutation: KRAS mutation is the dominant lung adenocarcinoma driver in this dataset, and TMED10 is a Golgi cargo-transport factor, so mutant KRAS lines may depend more strongly on secretory or membrane-traffic machinery. The expected raw contrast is more negative TMED10 dependency in KRAS-mutant versus wild-type lines, hence direction -1 and anticipated raw direction -1. Plausible alternatives are null if TMED10 is a general essential gene, or opposite if KRAS-mutant lines compensate through altered secretory traffic. Second, dependency_MDM2 by CDKN2A loss: CDKN2A encodes p14ARF as well as p16; ARF loss can enhance MDM2-mediated p53 control, so CDKN2A-loss lines may show stronger MDM2 dependency. The expected raw contrast is more negative MDM2 dependency in CDKN2A-loss lines, hence direction -1 and anticipated raw direction -1. Plausible alternatives are null if CDKN2A loss is dominated by p16 cell-cycle effects unrelated to MDM2, or opposite if CDKN2A loss co-occurs with TP53 loss and removes the MDM2-p53 dependency axis. These new tests remain exploratory and dataset-level. A clinically meaningful discovery would be a signed mean difference around 0.1 or larger with an interval away from zero; canonical effects are much larger, while small intervals near zero would support outcome or pathway specificity.

This analyze stage requests the twelve currently active, untested discovery comparisons that broaden the investigation to additional dependency outcomes while including specificity controls. The panel tests: RPL11 with TP53 loss; STAT3 with PIK3CA mutation, PTEN loss, and MYC amplification; KIF18A with RB1 loss, CDKN2A loss, and MYC amplification; TMED10 with ERBB2 amplification and KRAS mutation; MDM2 with CDKN2A loss; and DHX9/POLR2A with TP53 loss as specificity controls for the already-supported TP53-associated associations. These are selected because they cover plausible mechanistic axes: p53/RPL11 and p53/MDM2/ARF biology, PI3K/PTEN/MYC signaling with STAT3, cell-cycle/mitotic dependencies with RB1/CDKN2A/MYC and KIF18A, oncogenic driver/secretory traffic associations with KRAS/ERBB2 and TMED10, and transcriptional/RNA helicase controls with TP53. A meaningful positive finding would require an effect of at least roughly 0.1 dependency units with an interval away from zero, in line with the practical 10% benchmark; smaller or imprecise effects would be treated as null or unresolved rather than clinically meaningful. These remain dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

This panel mostly supports outcome and predictor specificity rather than broad TP53-related leakage. H48 RPL11 by TP53 loss is essentially null (signed +0.0037 [-0.0163, 0.0237]); I reject it. H66 PIK3CA mutation and H87 MYC amplification are both small nulls for STAT3 (signed -0.0136 [-0.0413, 0.0141] and -0.0041 [-0.0344, 0.0263]); reject both. H69 RB1 loss, H70 CDKN2A loss, and H88 MYC amplification are null for KIF18A (signed +0.0082, -0.0133, +0.0056 respectively); reject. H71 ERBB2 amplification and H93 KRAS mutation are null for TMED10 (signed +0.0013 and +0.0067); reject. H92 TP53 loss for POLR2A is small and nonsignificant (signed +0.0140 [-0.0057, 0.0338]); reject as no clinically meaningful evidence. H91 TP53 loss for DHX9 gives a statistically marginal but small signed effect -0.0201 [-0.0390, -0.0012], corresponding to a raw positive shift of about 0.020 (weakly weaker DHX9 dependency) and opposite the tested direction; it is small, unstable against the 10% benchmark, and not a robust clinically meaningful discovery, so I reject the tested claim. The main findings are H67 and H94. H67 PTEN loss gives signed +0.2674 [0.2153, 0.3195] for direction -1, meaning a raw mean difference of about -0.267: PTEN-loss lines have much stronger STAT3 dependency. This is large, statistically strong, and far exceeds the practical 10% benchmark on this score scale; I accept it but keep it active pending independent validation and context controls. H94 CDKN2A loss gives signed +0.1169 [0.0823, 0.1516] for direction -1, i.e. raw -0.117 stronger MDM2 dependency in CDKN2A-loss lines. This is also clinically meaningful and statistically robust, but biologically it could be mediated by p14ARF status, co-deletion, or TP53 context, so I accept it and keep it active with follow-up. Multiplicity is a concern because this was a 12-test discovery panel, but H67 and H94 have intervals far from zero and magnitudes large relative to the clinical benchmark, making simple false-positive explanations less plausible. I nevertheless request validation for H67 because it is the largest new discovery and could be sample-specific or confounded. H7 remains accepted but unvalidated; H94 needs TP53-context follow-up before any future validation decision.

H10 response deadline: validation R39 (signed +0.7925, independent interval +0.7627 to +0.8223) closely replicates discovery R10 (signed +0.7840, +0.7646 to +0.8034). Because H10 direction is -1, the raw SMARCA4-loss minus SMARCA4-intact contrast is negative, meaning SMARCA4-loss lines have stronger SMARCA2 dependency. This is decisive and far beyond the practical 0.1 dependency-unit threshold, so H10 remains accepted and closed. H67 validation R65 (signed +0.3288, independent interval +0.2553 to +0.4022) confirms discovery R55 (signed +0.2674, +0.2153 to +0.3195). With direction -1, PTEN-loss lines have a raw negative STAT3 dependency shift, i.e. stronger STAT3 dependency. The effect is robust after validation adjustment and exceeds the clinically meaningful benchmark; I accept H67 and close the direct claim while retaining context tests. With H13, H8, H10, and H67 now validated, the strongest dataset-level evidence supports KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and PTEN loss with stronger STAT3 dependency. H7 (TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency) and H94 (CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency) remain accepted associations, but H7 is unvalidated and H94 is modest (discovery estimate 0.117 with lower bound 0.082) and potentially confounded by TP53 or MTAP co-deletion; therefore the next panel evaluates p53 context, MTAP specificity, screen-quality robustness, and PTEN specificity. Negative controls support specificity: TP53 loss does not appreciably move SMARCA2, RPL11, POLR2A, or MDM2 overall; PIK3CA and MYC do not move STAT3; RB1, CDKN2A, and MYC do not move KIF18A; ERBB2 and KRAS do not move TMED10; KEAP1, SMARCA4, and MSI effects are not broad cell-state shifts in the tested cross-outcome controls; driver-matched oncogene dependencies were largely null. These are dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

No direct evidence assessments are due. To keep the next analysis budget focused at twelve active comparisons, I defer four lower-priority or partially redundant context controls: H95 STAT3/TP53 main effect, H96 PTEN effect in TP53 wild-type cells (partially recoverable from H97 and the H98 interaction), H104 STAT3/PTEN screen-quality robustness after H67 independent validation, and H106 USP7/TP53 within PTEN loss (covered by the PTEN specificity test H103). I add four falsifiable comparisons that broaden biology while clarifying an accepted but unvalidated association. BRCA2 loss is tested against WRN and DHX9 dependency because BRCA2-deficient genomes face replication stress, R-loop accumulation, and transcription-associated repair defects; these lines may depend more strongly on WRN or DHX9, giving more negative dependency scores. Plausible alternatives are null or opposite if BRCA2 loss bypasses these helicase pathways or collapses repair dependency. NF1 loss is tested against RIT1 dependency because NF1 loss activates RAS signaling, which may make lines more dependent on downstream RIT1 signaling; null or opposite results are also plausible. Finally, CDKN2A-loss is retested for MDM2 dependency restricted to MTAP-intact cells to test whether the H94 MDM2 association is not merely a 9p21 MTAP co-deletion artifact. Meaningful discoveries on these continuous dependency scores would generally require a contrast around 0.1 or larger with an interval away from zero; validated canonical effects are much larger. All conclusions remain dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

This analysis panel evaluates the twelve currently active, untested comparisons: PTEN-loss STAT3 dependency within TP53-loss context and the corresponding TP53-loss interaction (H97, H98); CDKN2A-loss MDM2 dependency across TP53 context, the TP53-loss interaction, the overall MTAP-loss association, MTAP-intact CDKN2A-loss specificity, and robustness in high-quality screens (H99-H102, H105, H110); USP7 dependency under PTEN loss as a specificity control for TP53-USP7 (H103); and mechanistically motivated new tests of BRCA2 loss with WRN and DHX9 dependency and NF1 loss with RIT1 dependency (H107-H109). All tests are two-group Welch contrasts within the specified eligibility populations. Signed estimates are already oriented to each claim direction. A meaningful positive dataset-level association would generally require a signed contrast of roughly 0.1 or larger with an interval away from zero, whereas validated canonical associations on this scale are substantially larger. Findings will be interpreted only as associations in this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable effects.

The new panel clarifies the PTEN–STAT3 and CDKN2A–MDM2 associations and tests several mechanistic specificity controls. For PTEN loss in TP53-loss cells, H97 gives signed +0.1903 with discovery interval [0.0851, 0.2955]; because the claim direction is -1, the raw contrast is negative, meaning TP53-loss/PTEN-loss lines have stronger STAT3 dependency. This is directionally consistent with the independently validated overall PTEN–STAT3 effect, supports a genuine subgroup effect, and I accept it, while noting that the lower bound is just below the practical 0.1 benchmark because the TP53-loss exposed cell has only 54 lines. H98 tests whether that effect is stronger in TP53-loss cells; its signed estimate is -0.0967 with interval [-0.2171, 0.0236], crossing zero and pointing in the opposite direction. I therefore reject H98 as no evidence of a TP53-loss interaction. This does not contradict H97: H97 shows the effect exists in the TP53-loss context, whereas the interaction is too imprecise and not clinically compelling. I have activated H96 to test the complementary TP53-wildtype PTEN context later.

The CDKN2A–MDM2 follow-up is coherent. H99 in TP53-wildtype lines gives signed +0.1185 [0.0793, 0.1577], indicating raw stronger MDM2 dependency with CDKN2A loss; I accept it. H100 in TP53-loss lines gives signed +0.1106 [0.0350, 0.1862]; it excludes zero and has a clinically meaningful point estimate, but the lower bound is uncertain and below 0.1. I accept it as consistent subgroup evidence while treating it as less precise than H99. H101, the corresponding TP53-loss interaction, is essentially null at signed -0.0079 [-0.0928, 0.0770], so I reject any claim that TP53 status modifies the CDKN2A effect. MTAP is also not an obvious confounder: H102 MTAP loss overall is small and null, signed +0.0186 [-0.0078, 0.0450], and H110 CDKN2A loss within MTAP-intact cells remains clinically meaningful, signed +0.1049 [0.0669, 0.1430]. H105 in higher-quality screens is also robust, signed +0.1319 [0.0910, 0.1727]. Taken with the already accepted overall H94 effect, these results make 9p21 MTAP co-deletion or TP53-context confounding less plausible and support CDKN2A/p14ARF-related MDM2 specificity. I therefore keep H94 accepted and request independent validation for H94.

The remaining new tests are nulls and support specificity rather than broad dependency shifts. USP7 dependency under PTEN loss is null and slightly opposite to a generalized p53/USP7-like leakage pattern, signed -0.0173 [-0.0654, 0.0308]; reject H103. BRCA2 loss is null for WRN and DHX9, signed -0.0001 [-0.0449, 0.0448] and +0.0121 [-0.0197, 0.0439], and NF1 loss is null for RIT1, signed -0.0206 [-0.0487, 0.0075]; reject H107-H109. These reject plausible replication-stress/R-loop/RAS-pathway associations in this dataset. Multiplicity remains a concern, but the accepted effects are internally consistent across context and specificity tests, whereas nearby cross-outcome controls are null. I also activate H73 as a screen-quality robustness test for the large accepted TP53–USP7 association, while prioritizing validation of H94. All conclusions remain dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

H8 response deadline: independent validation R52 gives signed +0.8019 [0.7533, 0.8506], closely matching discovery R8 (+0.7899 [0.7604, 0.8193]). With direction -1, MSI-high lines have much stronger WRN dependency. This is decisive and closes H8 as a validated dataset-level association. H94 is now independently validated: discovery R62 was +0.1169 [0.0823, 0.1516], and validation R78 is +0.1299 [0.0751, 0.1848]. With direction -1, CDKN2A-loss lines have stronger MDM2 dependency. The validation interval excludes zero and the point estimate is above the practical 0.1 benchmark, though the lower bound is near that benchmark. Combined with the prior context tests showing stability across TP53 status, MTAP-intact cells, and high-quality screens, and no evidence for TP53 interaction, I accept and close H94 as a moderate but reproducible CDKN2A-specific MDM2 association. H35 tests whether Avana library exposure itself moves USP7 dependency. Validation R79 is small and nonsignificant, signed +0.0326 [-0.0349, 0.1002], so I reject it and close it. This supports specificity for the large H7 TP53-loss USP7 association by arguing against a broad Avana-library artifact. I keep H7 accepted but active because it is the largest remaining accepted unvalidated association. I have activated H73 for screen-quality robustness, H96 for PTEN loss within TP53-wildtype STAT3 context, and H50 plus H16 as TP53-USP7 robustness contexts in non-Avana screens and adenocarcinoma lines. The next analyses should focus on whether H7 persists in cleaner and more specific subpopulations and whether H96 confirms that PTEN-STAT3 is not confined to TP53-loss context. All claims remain dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable conclusions.

No evidence assessments are due. I keep the currently active focused follow-ups for the accepted but unvalidated TP53-USP7 association (H16, H50, H73) and the PTEN-STAT3 context test (H96). I add five falsifiable comparisons that broaden biology while providing specificity checks. First, STK11 and SMAD4 losses are common lung adenocarcinoma co-mutations that can alter metabolic stress, inflammatory signaling, and TGF-beta rewiring; both could make cells more dependent on STAT3, which would appear as a more negative STAT3 dependency score and correspond to a negative raw exposed-minus-comparator contrast. The alternative is that the PTEN-STAT3 finding is pathway-specific or that STK11/SMAD4 effects are null or opposite in these lines. Second, MSI-high was validated as strongly associated with WRN dependency; I now test DHX9 and POLR2A to ask whether MSI marks a broader replication/transcription vulnerability or whether the effect is WRN-specific in this dataset. Third, KRAS mutation is a major RAS-pathway exposure, and STAT3 is a plausible downstream inflammatory effector, so I test STAT3 despite previous KRAS-associated controls being null. For these continuous dependency scores, I will treat an absolute contrast around 0.1 or larger with an interval away from zero as scientifically meaningful, while acknowledging that validated canonical associations in this dataset are much larger. These proposals are designed to be active alongside existing tests but not saturate the twelve-analysis budget. H7 validation will be decided at appraisal after its robustness contexts are examined.

This analysis panel targets currently active follow-up questions and three deferred comparisons whose direct subgroup estimates are now useful. First, it tests the accepted but unvalidated TP53-loss USP7 association H7 in four contexts: adenocarcinoma lines (H16), non-Avana screens (H50), Avana screens (H44), and higher-quality screens with screen_roc_auc at least 0.93 (H73). Direct estimates in these contexts are complementary to the earlier rejected library and screen-quality interactions: they ask whether the effect is present within each major technical or biological context, not only whether the context changes the contrast. Positive signed estimates for these +1-direction claims would mean TP53-loss lines have weaker USP7 dependency, consistent with H7. Second, H96 tests PTEN loss and STAT3 dependency within TP53-wildtype cells; together with the already accepted TP53-loss subgroup H97 and independently validated overall H67, this clarifies whether PTEN-STAT3 is a broad association rather than one confined to a TP53 context. Third, the panel evaluates newly registered STAT3 associations under STK11 loss (H111), SMAD4 loss (H112), and KRAS mutation (H115), testing lung adenocarcinoma co-mutational/inflammatory/RAS-pathway hypotheses. Fourth, H113 and H114 test whether the independently validated MSI-high WRN association is part of a broader DHX9 or POLR2A replication/transcription vulnerability, or whether it is WRN-specific in this dataset. Finally, H74 and H75 activate direct robustness estimates for the validated SMARCA4-SMARCA2 and MSI-WRN associations in high-quality screens. For all dependency-score claims, a signed estimate around 0.1 or larger with an interval away from zero would be treated as meaningful dataset-level evidence; smaller positive estimates may be accepted as supportive but imprecise, while intervals near zero or opposite signs will not support the claim. Validated canonical associations in this dataset are much larger, so context-specific attenuation will be considered carefully. All findings remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable effects.

The new panel strongly supports the remaining accepted but unvalidated TP53-USP7 association and independently confirms the PTEN-STAT3 association in a second TP53 context. For USP7, the claim direction is +1, so a positive signed estimate means TP53-loss cells have a less negative, weaker USP7 dependency score. H16 in adenocarcinoma gives +0.7990 [0.7755, 0.8225], H44 in Avana screens gives +0.8057 [0.7851, 0.8263], H73 in high-quality screens with screen_roc_auc at least 0.93 gives +0.8079 [0.7855, 0.8304], and H50 in non-Avana screens gives +0.7674 [0.7031, 0.8318]. All four are far above the 0.1 practical benchmark and have intervals excluding zero. H50 is less precise because only 43 exposed lines contribute, but the lower bound remains extremely large, so I accept it while treating it as a smaller, noisier robustness check. These context-specific results are internally consistent with the rejected library and screen-quality interactions: the association is not explained by one major library or screen-quality stratum. H7 remains the largest accepted unvalidated association, and the convergence across technical and biological contexts makes independent validation of H7 now the highest-value validation request.

PTEN loss within TP53-wildtype cells, H96, gives signed +0.2870 [0.2273, 0.3467] for dependency_STAT3 with direction -1. Because the direction is -1, the raw contrast is negative, meaning PTEN-loss TP53-wildtype lines have a more negative STAT3 dependency score, i.e. stronger STAT3 dependency. This is clinically meaningful, excludes zero, and complements the independently validated overall PTEN-STAT3 result H67 and the TP53-loss subgroup H97. The pattern supports a broad dataset-level PTEN-STAT3 association rather than a TP53-context artifact. I accept and close H96.

The newly activated specificity controls are null. STK11 loss and STAT3 dependency is +0.0145 [-0.0137, 0.0427] (H111), SMAD4 loss and STAT3 is +0.0109 [-0.0257, 0.0475] (H112), MSI-high and DHX9 is +0.0172 [-0.0174, 0.0517] (H113), MSI-high and POLR2A is -0.0035 [-0.0348, 0.0277] (H114), and KRAS mutation and STAT3 is -0.0175 [-0.0418, 0.0068] (H115). All have absolute estimates far below the 0.1 benchmark and intervals compatible with no effect; the KRAS estimate also points away from the claimed stronger-dependency direction. I reject all five and close them. These results argue against a broad STAT3 co-mutational or RAS-pathway pattern in this dataset and support WRN-specificity of the MSI-high effect, since MSI was not associated with DHX9 or POLR2A.

Finally, the high-quality-screen robustness checks for validated associations are clear. H74 shows SMARCA4 loss remains associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, signed +0.7895 [0.7676, 0.8114]; H75 shows MSI-high remains associated with stronger WRN dependency, signed +0.7924 [0.7599, 0.8249]. Both are accepted and closed as dataset-level consistency checks. Overall, the evidence favors a focused set of robust associations: TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency, PTEN loss with stronger STAT3 dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, and CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency. Multiplicity is mitigated by consistency across independent contexts and by the null specificity controls. I request validation of H7 to address the largest accepted unvalidated association. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

H7 is now independently validated. Discovery R7 gave a signed estimate of +0.8019 [0.7823, 0.8216], and validation R92 gives +0.7904 [0.7615, 0.8194] at the validation alpha level. Because the claim direction is +1, the positive raw exposed-minus-comparator difference means TP53-loss lines have a less negative USP7 dependency score, i.e. weaker USP7 dependency. The validation interval is tight, excludes zero, and is extremely large relative to the 0.1 practical benchmark for dependency-score contrasts. Combined with the prior consistency across adenocarcinoma lines, Avana and non-Avana screens, high-quality screens, rejected library/screen-quality interactions, and the rejected broad Avana-library main effect, I accept H7 and close it as a validated dataset-level association. It is an association within this supplied dataset, not a causal claim or generalizable biological rule.

H67 response deadline: independent validation R65 gives a signed estimate of +0.3288 [0.2553, 0.4022] for PTEN loss versus STAT3 dependency, compared with discovery R55 of +0.2674 [0.2153, 0.3195]. The claim direction is -1, so the underlying raw contrast is negative: PTEN-loss lines have a more negative STAT3 dependency score, i.e. stronger STAT3 dependency. The validation interval excludes zero and the point estimate is well above the practical 0.1 benchmark. This is reinforced by the accepted TP53-wildtype context H96, the accepted TP53-loss context H97, and the rejected TP53-loss interaction H98. I therefore accept and close H67 as a validated dataset-level PTEN-STAT3 association, again only within this dataset and not as causal or generalizable.

With TP53-USP7, PTEN-STAT3, KEAP1-NFE2L2, SMARCA4-SMARCA2, MSI-high-WRN, and CDKN2A-MDM2 now validated or robustly supported, the next highest-value work is focused specificity and one underexplored pathway. I activate H95 to test whether TP53 loss also has a broad STAT3 association. Given that PTEN-STAT3 is not driven by a TP53 interaction and TP53-USP7 is highly selective, I expect H95 to be null, but it is a useful p53-pathway specificity test. I activate H104 to test PTEN-STAT3 within high-quality screens, completing a robustness check for the validated PTEN effect. I also activate H68, MYC amplification versus RPL11 dependency, and register a related new proposal, CDKN2A loss versus RPL11 dependency. RPL11 is biologically adjacent to MDM2 and p53 regulation; CDKN2A loss already predicts stronger MDM2 dependency, so testing RPL11 may reveal whether the CDKN2A association has p53-pathway specificity or extends to related ribosomal stress machinery. If these tests are null or below the practical benchmark, they will further sharpen the accepted set. If any meaningful effect emerges, it will require context checks before validation. All current conclusions remain dataset-level associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

No evidence assessments are due at this explore stage. The current evidence supports a focused set of dataset-level associations: TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency, PTEN loss with stronger STAT3 dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, and CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency. Many targeted null tests already provide specificity controls, so the next useful scientific step is to balance focused refinement of these associations with a limited set of new mechanistic probes.

I propose three new main-effect hypotheses. First, RB1 loss and WRN dependency are biologically linked: RB1 loss derepresses E2F targets and can increase replication stress, which would plausibly make WRN more essential and produce a more negative dependency score; the alternative is that RB1 loss does not impose WRN-specific replication stress in these lines. Second, NF1 loss and KRAS dependency test RAS-pathway essentiality after NF1 loss, a RASGAP loss condition. The direction is registered as stronger KRAS dependency, but the expectation is deliberately agnostic because NF1 loss may either increase RAS-pathway dependence or bypass KRAS-specific dependency. Third, ERBB2 amplification and dependency_EGFR test ERBB-family redundancy: HER2 amplification could reduce EGFR dependency by providing redundant signaling, whereas co-dependent ERBB family biology could instead produce a null or opposite result. For the EGFR claim, direction +1 means a positive signed estimate corresponds to weaker EGFR dependency in HER2-amplified lines.

I also register five context-specific interactions that refine already supported associations. SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 dependency is tested within ARID1A co-loss, because co-compromised SWI/SNF complexes may make SMARCA2 more essential; the alternative is that ARID1A loss buffers or does not modify this vulnerability. KEAP1 loss effect on NFE2L2 dependency is tested within SMARCA4 loss, because chromatin remodeling state could modify NRF2 transcriptional output; the KEAP1 main effect is robust, but the interaction asks whether it is amplified, attenuated, or unchanged. CDKN2A loss effect on MDM2 dependency is tested within MYC amplification, a common co-alteration that could increase proliferation/replication stress and strengthen MDM2 dependence, although epistasis may erase the effect. MSI-high effect on WRN dependency is tested within STK11 loss, another metabolic/replication stress context that could synergize with microsatellite replication stress. Finally, PTEN loss effect on STAT3 dependency is tested within STK11 loss because combined PI3K-AKT and metabolic perturbations could amplify STAT3 survival dependence, while the prior STK11 main effect was null, making this a focused epistasis test rather than a broad claim.

I include three direct specificity or adjacency tests. STK11 loss and MDM2 dependency test whether metabolic stress alters the p53-MDM2 axis beyond CDKN2A deletion. MTAP loss and RPL11 dependency test the CDKN2A/MDM2 adjacency network: MTAP deletion often co-occurs with CDKN2A deletion, and RPL11 is biologically adjacent to MDM2-p53 ribosomal stress signaling. APC mutation and STAT3 dependency is a Wnt-crosstalk/specificity check; the expectation is uncertain, and a null result would further support the specificity of PTEN-STAT3. Across all new proposals, I will treat absolute dependency-score contrasts near or above roughly 0.1 with intervals away from zero as meaningful, while recognizing that validated canonical associations here are much larger, around 0.8 for the main effects and around 0.1-0.3 for moderate CDKN2A-MDM2 and PTEN-STAT3 effects. These are registered as dataset-level associations and not as causal or generalizable claims.

No evidence assessments are due. I request 12 untested active comparisons, deferring H68, H125, and H127 only because of the 12-comparison analysis budget. The panel has four scientific purposes. First, it strengthens the accepted STAT3 specificity/robustness set by testing TP53 loss on STAT3 dependency, H95, and PTEN loss on STAT3 dependency within high-quality screens, H104. Given the currently selective TP53-USP7 and PTEN-STAT3 associations, a null H95 and stable H104 would be informative. Second, it tests RPL11 as a biologically adjacent outcome to the accepted CDKN2A-MDM2 association: H116 tests CDKN2A loss directly on RPL11 dependency, and H126 tests MTAP loss, a common co-deleted marker, to distinguish CDKN2A-region signal from co-deletion confounding. H68, MYC amplification on RPL11, is deferred because MYC has been null for several related dependency outcomes and H122 more directly tests MYC as a modifier of CDKN2A-MDM2 biology. Third, it tests three new mechanistic main effects: H117 RB1 loss on WRN dependency, H118 NF1 loss on KRAS dependency, and H119 ERBB2 amplification on EGFR dependency. These probe replication-stress and ERBB-pathway vulnerability hypotheses not covered by existing nulls. Fourth, it evaluates context modification of accepted associations through H120 SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 within ARID1A co-loss, H121 KEAP1-loss effect on NFE2L2 within SMARCA4 loss, H122 CDKN2A-loss effect on MDM2 within MYC amplification, H123 MSI-high effect on WRN within STK11 loss, and H124 PTEN-loss effect on STAT3 within STK11 loss. For dependency-score contrasts, signed estimates around 0.1 or larger with intervals excluding zero will be treated as meaningful dataset-level evidence, while validated canonical effects are much larger. Interactions will be interpreted as context-specific modification of the main association; large interactions should prompt context-specific mean-difference checks before validation. All conclusions will remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

This panel mostly strengthens the specificity of the accepted association set rather than revealing new drivers. H95 tests TP53 loss on STAT3 dependency with direction -1, meaning that a positive signed estimate would support stronger STAT3 dependency in TP53-loss lines. The observed signed estimate is -0.0124 [-0.0370, 0.0121], which is tiny, crosses zero, and points away from the proposed stronger-dependency direction. I reject and close H95. The new proposals focus on two axes that are not yet fully mapped: the MDM2/p53 stress axis and the STAT3 upstream-crosstalk axis, plus one specificity check for the USP7 association.

First, MYC amplification can generate ribosome-biogenesis and replication/proliferation stress, often engaging ARF-MDM2-p53 responses. I therefore test MYC amplification against MDM2 dependency within TP53-wildtype lines. This context is chosen because a MYC-MDM2 relationship would be most expected when p53 is intact. The claim direction is -1: a positive signed estimate would mean MYC-amplified TP53-wildtype lines have a more negative MDM2 dependency score, i.e. stronger MDM2 dependency. If this is null, it would strengthen the specificity of CDKN2A-MDM2 rather than suggesting a broad p53-axis MDM2 association.

Second, PTEN loss activates PI3K-AKT signaling and can modulate MDM2 activity through AKT-mediated phosphorylation. I test PTEN loss against MDM2 dependency, again within TP53-wildtype lines, because MDM2 dependency is likely most interpretable when p53 pathway output is preserved. The direction is -1, with an uncertain anticipated raw direction. A positive signed estimate would indicate stronger MDM2 dependency in PTEN-loss/TP53-wildtype lines; a null result would help confine the PTEN association to STAT3 and reduce concern that PTEN loss causes broad p53-axis dependency changes.

Third, the validated PTEN-STAT3 association invites testing whether STAT3 dependency is a broader node for other growth-factor/RAS/NRF2 pathway perturbations. I test NF1 loss against STAT3 dependency with direction -1 because NF1 loss can increase RAS/MAPK signaling and may produce stronger STAT3 dependence. I also test ERBB2 amplification against STAT3 dependency with direction -1 because HER2-amplified cells can activate STAT3-associated survival signaling. Both would be meaningful if they produce signed estimates well away from zero and around or above the practical 0.1 dependency-score scale, but they are also useful as specificity controls if null: the PTEN-STAT3 association may be pathway-selective rather than a general RTK/RAS signal.

Fourth, I test KEAP1 loss against STAT3 dependency. NRF2 and STAT3 can interact through oxidative-stress and inflammatory-survival programs, but the expected direction is uncertain. The claim is registered with direction -1 so that a positive signed result would indicate stronger STAT3 dependency in KEAP1-loss lines. A positive result would be a new potential primary association; a null result would reinforce that KEAP1 loss is strongly specific for the NFE2L2 dependency phenotype rather than a broad transcriptional-survival dependency effect.

Finally, I test CDKN2A loss against USP7 dependency. TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency, and CDKN2A alteration can affect p53-axis stress signaling through ARF loss. The claim direction is +1: a positive signed estimate would indicate weaker USP7 dependency in CDKN2A-loss lines, analogous to the TP53-loss USP7 direction. The expected raw direction is uncertain. A null result would sharpen the specificity of TP53-loss USP7 dependency and separate the CDKN2A-MDM2 association from a broader USP7/p53-axis effect.

Across these proposals, I will treat signed dependency-score contrasts around 0.1 or larger, with intervals away from zero, as scientifically meaningful for this dependency-score scale, while recognizing that validated canonical effects here can be much larger. Any newly strong result should prompt either a context-specific follow-up or validation. All claims remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

These remain dataset associations, not causal statements.

The new validation for H150 supports the refined CDKN2A-loss MDM2-dependency context. H150 tests CDKN2A loss versus CDKN2A-intact cells within TP53-loss, MTAP-wildtype lines. The direction is -1, so a positive signed estimate means the CDKN2A-loss group has a more negative MDM2 dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency. Discovery R130 was +0.0998 with a 95% Welch interval +0.0182 to +0.1815. Independent validation R142 is +0.1459 with adjusted independent interval +0.0231 to +0.2687 at alpha 0.00385, in cells with n=73 exposed and n=241 comparator. The independent interval excludes zero, the effect is in the hypothesized direction, and the point estimate exceeds the practical 0.1 scale and is consistent with a 10% relative practical difference for these dependency scores. I therefore accept H150 and close it. This supports an association in the supplied lung cell-line dataset: within TP53-loss lines that are MTAP-wildtype, CDKN2A loss is associated with stronger MDM2 dependency. This is not a causal statement, not a therapeutic claim, and not a claim of external generalizability. It also does not retroactively establish the broader TP53-loss-only H100 claim: H100 remains unresolved/closed because its independent validation R105 crossed zero and was below the practical benchmark. The clean H150 context is important because it reduces the possibility that the TP53-loss subgroup result is purely driven by MTAP co-deletion, but the exact TP53-loss-only context remains uncertain.

Current supported primary dataset associations, with independent validation where available, are: TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency, H7 R7 +0.802 and R92 +0.790; KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, H13 R9 +0.796 and R26 +0.806; SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, H10 R10 +0.784 and R39 +0.793; MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, H8 R8 +0.790 and R52 +0.802; PTEN loss with stronger STAT3 dependency, H67 R55 +0.267 and R65 +0.329; and CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency overall, H94 R62 +0.117 and R78 +0.130. The newly accepted H150 refines the MDM2 association by showing persistence in a TP53-loss, MTAP-wildtype background.

Several context-specific acceptances further show that the accepted associations are not confined to one technical or biological stratum in this dataset. TP53-loss USP7 effects persist in adenocarcinoma H16/R80, Avana library H44/R83, non-Avana library H50/R81, high screen quality H73/R82, and high Cas9 activity H156/R136. KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 effects persist within TP53-loss H56/R35, within KEAP1-loss USP7 context H57/R36, and in high aneuploidy H158/R138. SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 effects persist in TP53-wildtype, KEAP1-wildtype, MSI-wildtype lines H31/R17, TP53-loss lines H58/R37, high screen quality H74/R90, adherent culture H151/R131, matched RNA-DNA omics H152/R132, and ARID1A-loss H153/R133. MSI-high WRN effects persist in adenocarcinoma H15/R141, TP53- and KEAP1-wildtype lines H32/R18, high screen quality H75/R91, high serum H154/R134, and near-diploid backgrounds H155/R135. PTEN-loss STAT3 effects persist in TP53-wildtype H96/R84, TP53-loss H97/R66, high screen quality H104/R94, and high ploidy H157/R137. CDKN2A-loss MDM2 effects persist in TP53-wildtype lines H99/R68, high screen quality H105/R73, MTAP-wildtype lines H110/R77, and high mutation burden H159/R139, and now in the TP53-loss, MTAP-wildtype context H150/R130 and R142.

The negative and specificity findings are also substantial. Most canonical driver or receptor-tyrosine-kinase genotype probes were near null for the corresponding dependencies: KRAS mutation did not show a meaningful KRAS-dependency difference H1/R1, BRAF V600E did not show a meaningful BRAF-dependency difference H2/R2, EGFR amplification did not show a validated practical EGFR-dependency difference H3/R3 and R13, ERBB2 amplification did not show a meaningful ERBB2-dependency difference H4/R4, and NF1 loss was not meaningfully associated with RIT1 dependency H5/R5 or other tested dependencies H109/R76, H118/R97, H136/R119. Cross-pathway probes generally did not extend accepted associations to unrelated dependencies: KEAP1 loss did not meaningfully affect USP7 H41/R24 or SMARCA2 H64/R106; SMARCA4 loss did not meaningfully affect USP7 H65/R107, WRN H42/R25, or POLR2A H141/R124; TP53 loss did not meaningfully affect WRN H144/R125, NFE2L2 H146/R126, STAT3 H95/R93, RPL11 H48/R53, or DHX9 in the practical hypothesized direction H91/R63; PTEN loss did not meaningfully affect USP7 H103/R72 or MDM2 in TP53-wildtype lines H130/R113. MYC amplification was null for DHX9 H11/R11, POLR2A H12/R12, RPL11 H68/R108, KIF18A H88/R59, and STAT3 H87/R56. BRCA2 loss was null for WRN H107/R74 and DHX9 H108/R75; MSI-high was null for DHX9 H113/R87 and POLR2A H114/R88; RB1 loss was null for KIF18A H69/R57 and WRN H117/R96; CDKN2A loss was null for KIF18A H70/R58 and RPL11 H116/R95. Many interaction tests were negative, including lineage subtype H25/R27, H26/R28, H27/R29, H28/R30, screen batch H52/R31, H53/R32, H54/R33, H55/R34, screen-quality interactions H80/R44, H81/R45, H82/R46, H83/R47, co-alteration interactions H76/R40, H77/R41, H78/R42, H79/R43, H84/R48, H85/R49, H86/R50, H98/R67, H101/R70, H120/R99, H121/R100, H122/R101, H123/R102, H124/R103, and library/library-context probes H33/R19, H34/R20, H35/R21 and R79, H20/R14. Research markers D, E, and F were mostly null where tested, including H18/R22, H20/R14, and H36/R23. These nulls increase confidence that the accepted large effects are relatively specific dataset associations rather than broad technical, lineage, or assay artifacts.

Remaining uncertainty is mainly contextual. H100, the exact TP53-loss-only CDKN2A-MDM2 comparison, remains unresolved/closed: discovery R69 was positive but independent validation R105 crossed zero. H160 remains unresolved/closed: within CDKN2A-loss lines, MTAP co-loss did not show a credible additional effect, but the interval R140 +0.064, -0.025 to +0.153, is too wide to claim precise absence. Several conditional acceptances are robust but depend on subgroup sample sizes and should not be generalized beyond the supplied lung-cell-line dataset. The most informative next registered analyses are: first, an MDM2 CDKN2A-by-TP53 interaction among MTAP-wildtype lines, to test whether TP53 status still modifies the CDKN2A-MDM2 association after removing MTAP co-deletion confounding; and second, SMARCA4-loss association with stronger SMARCA2 dependency in ARID1A-wildtype lines, to test whether the SWI/SNF context is independent of ARID1A co-loss.
